thread.title: Apple Vs. Bank Of America: Tariffs Vs. Rising Interest Rates - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Kwan-Chen Ma
title: Apple Vs. Bank Of America: Tariffs Vs. Rising Interest Rates - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
By K C Ma and Humberto J Soares
In many of our recent posts on SA, we encountered much readers’ resistance to acknowledge the negative impact from tariffs on stocks in the better part of 2018. The 2018 stock market has evidenced a lackluster performance even with a historical high level of economic activity. Many critics dismiss the tariffs impact and attribute the low stock returns to the rising interest rates. In this post, we aim to explore the main reasons for the 2018 stock performance.
Tariffs Impact To estimate the impact of tariffs on stock prices, we cannot simply compare the changes in stock prices after the tariffs have been imposed. This is due to company fundamentals changing over time -- stock prices would have changed regardless of the existence of tariffs. Simply looking at the stock price changes after tariffs changes does not give a clear picture of the tariffs impact. Therefore, our thinking process is as follows: In order to estimate the impact of tariffs and rising interest rates, we need to first identify how the stocks in question are priced in an environment of no tariffs and low interest rates (before 2018). This process is referred as a “tariff-free” pricing process. When we applied this pricing process to the time period of 2018, the resulting price estimates on 2018 financials would approximate the “what-if” stock price if the tariffs have never happened. When we compared the what-if prices with the actual stock prices, the differences would be a good approximation for the impact of tariffs.
Tariffs-Free Pricing Process Since stock prices are forward looking, we selected several typical forward financial metrics. These metrics include Street consensus estimates for quarterly revenue, earnings per share, free cash flow, and gross margin over the last five years with daily values. More importantly, since rising interest rates are a competing argument to explain stock prices, the 10-year Treasury rate was also included as one of the metrics used to estimate stock price movement. Then, for each stock, we developed a market pricing structure by correlating stock prices with their corresponding forward financials for the period before 2018, i.e., 2011-2017. Remember, this is the time period before the tariffs were imposed and interest rates started to rise. A significant correlation would imply the process of how the market has priced these firms' fundamentals. Using this process, we were able to estimate each one of the stocks' target prices in 2018.
Stocks of Interest Since tariffs and rising interest rates have been the commonly cited reasons for the 2018 market performance, we examined a number of stocks which are known to be the most affected by these factors.
Walmart
On Sept. 17, the U.S. imposed a 10% tariff on 200 billion dollars worth of Chinese goods. The rate of the tariff will be raised to 25% at year-end. A total of 5,745 Chinese goods are targeted. On Sept. 18, China responded with a 5%-10% tariff on 60 billion dollars worth of U.S. goods. U.S. goods amounted to 5,207. Given the expansive nature of the U.S. tariffs, Walmart ( NYSE: WMT ) is most vulnerable to both Trump's tariffs and China's retaliation.
Using the procedure described above, we were able to estimate what the Walmart tariffs-free stock price (in red) would have looked like, relative to the actual Walmart stock price (Figure 1A). It appears that the actual Walmart price trades at a 15%-20% discount to the theoretical tariffs-free price, after the first tariffs were announced in early 2018. The discount may approximate the adverse tariffs impact currently being priced in by Walmart shareholders.
Ford
Ford (NYSE: F ) was selected because it has everything to lose from the U.S. steel and aluminum tariffs as well as China’s retaliation tariffs on imported U.S. automobiles. Ford CEO Jim Hackett recently announced that the steel and aluminum tariffs have cost the company over $1 billion, CNBC also reported that the nations’ large retailers should not worry too much about the cost increase until the end of the year, due to the already overstock of Chinese imports. For Ford’s case, the perceived tariffs impact has been priced in at the order of -20% to -25% (Figure 1B). In comparison, the relative larger discount may suggest that the market price has reflected both the imported steel cost increase, as well as the future demand decrease for Ford’s trucks in China due to Chinese retaliation tariffs on US cars.
Apple
We look at Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) as a “control” case to show the tariffs impact or better yet, a lack of such. This is because Apple is the only tech firm that received the White House’s blessing to be exempted from US tariffs on Chinese imports. As expected, and happily for Apple, both the Apple Watch and Air Pods have been left off the list of products that will be subject to 10% import tariffs from September 24. The NY Times notes that they were among 300 product lines removed from an earlier draft. Among the items dropped are smart watches, Bluetooth devices, bike helmets, plastic gloves, high chairs, play pens and certain chemicals. Apple’s lack of immediate tariffs’ risk is further confirmed by the lack of the “tariffs discount” in its stock price, which is clearly observed in the case of Walmart and Ford (Figure 2). The contrasting evidence of tariffs discount also serves a validation of the argument:Tariffs are the ones to account for the lackluster stock prices performance in 2018.
Bank of America
Considering the impact of rising interest rates, we also looked at Bank of America (NYSE: BAC ) given that financial firms or banks are mostly sensitive to interest rate changes. Fundamentally, Bank of America (by being part of the financial industry), is supposed to be most benefited from a rising interest rate environment. However, it is surprising to note that Bank of America stock still trades at a significant discount, around 20%, to its theoretical tariffs-free price level (Figure 1C). As general interest rate levels have been rising, BAC’s sub-par performance cannot be explained by the interest rate moves -- Bank of America or U.S. financial industry is clearly not subject to any direct or immediate tariffs. One likely possibility is that the market has priced in the forthcoming recession scenario when tariffs turn into a trade war. In other words, BAC’s lack of interest rate connection further strengthens the argument of a negative tariffs impact to the overall stock market in 2018.
Tariffs Impact Is Real! For Walmart and Ford, which are clearly affected by the current tariffs, we found that their stocks are traded at a significant 20%-25% discount to the levels if there were no tariffs. For Apple, a stock which is exempted from the tariffs, we found no such discount. As a result of the difference, we can naturally conclude that there is a negative tariffs impact on most affected U.S. stock prices. For Bank of America, a company that is supposed to prosper in a rising interest rate environment, its stock also trades at a similar discount. Both the contrasting and similar evidence leads us to believe that the tariffs effect, not the rising interest rate, is the main driving force for 2018 lackluster U.S. stock performance.
That being said, there is bad news and there is good news. The bad news is that, by now, it is abundantly clear that trade tariffs and the looming trade war have produced a negative impact on all U. S. stockholders, regardless of whether their companies are on the tariffs lists.
Furthermore, there has not yet been a significant real impact from tariffs on both the top line revenue and bottom line earnings. It is estimated that first run of tariffs will show up in the U.S. firms’ financials after Q4 2018.
The good news is that, to shareholders of the affected companies, the “damages” have been confined to the speculation of the future impact and the duration of the trade war conflict, more of a “trade war risk premium.”
Given some early sign of weakening stances between U.S. and China on the trade policy, the end may be in sight, and the end may return the shareholders that 20%-25% trade war risk premium.
Disclosure: I/we have no positions in any stocks mentioned, and no plans to initiate any positions within the next 72 hours.
